dedupe_keys.name: amphibious houses in the maas floodplain at maasbommel netherlands climate adapt

description: This Climate-ADAPT case study describes the first amphibious houses built in the Netherlands, in a designated flood zone of the river Maas at Maasbommel. The developer Dura Vermeer, with Factor Architecten and the engineers Boiten, designed houses with a hollow concrete base and a light timber frame that are moored to steel posts and can float up by as much as 5.5 metres; escape routes also had to work with the house afloat, and the design had to meet the National Water Act. The houses were designed between 1998 and 2004 and built in 2004-2005, and they first floated in 2011 when the Maas rose, with no problems reported. They sold for about EUR 320,000 each, with a 15-year guarantee on floating. Coverage: one riverside development, with KNMI14 projections of higher Maas discharges to 2085. Access: the case study page, first published on 7 June 2016 and modified on 25 August 2026, with the architect's project page. Licence: Climate-ADAPT content under the EEA reuse policy; free. Caveats: the houses are recreational homes and costs were high because every element was bespoke; no measured flood performance data are given beyond the 2011 event. Simulation uses are a reference for floodplain housing design in exposure and loss models, where amphibious buildings change depth-damage assumptions. Related records: the Eferdinger Becken relocation and Bilbao Zorrotzaurre case studies.
name: Amphibious houses in the Maas floodplain at Maasbommel, Netherlands (Climate-ADAPT)
outcomes: Amphibious houses on hollow concrete bases moored to steel posts can rise up to 5.5 m; they floated without problems for the first time in 2011. They sold for about EUR 320,000 with a 15-year floating guarantee, and the project won the 2010 Water Wonen & Ruimte Award.
